description: Wayne Allyn Root review, checked 20 Nov 2026: $30 VegasWinners picks, no refunds, unverified streak claims, and what Winners, Inc. now tells the SEC.
dek: Wayne Allyn Root ran the Winning Edge pick business in the 2000s and still sells picks on VegasWinners.com, where a single pick costs $30. The site markets win streaks but publishes no full pick log, its refund policy says no refunds, and its parent company now describes itself to the SEC as pre revenue under a new chief executive.

short_answer: Wayne Allyn Root is a real, long known handicapper and broadcaster. Filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission show he was chief executive of Winning Edge International, a public company that sold handicapping advice until it sold its operating assets in 2007. He later ran Winners, Inc., whose VegasWinners.com still sells his picks for $30 each with a listed phone number.

Whether his picks make money is not something we could check. The site shows short streaks and season highlights from 2017 to 2020, chosen by the seller, with no log of every pick, line and post time. A 2021 company press release said all of his picks are "independently monitored and documented" without naming who does it. His own pick write up on 20 Nov 2026 opened with "0-2", while his profile header still advertised a 7 and 1 streak.

The business around him has shrunk. Winners, Inc. told the SEC in October 2026 that it is a "pre-revenue early development-stage company" with $594 of revenue in the first half of 2026, now run by a different chief executive through a sports analytics subsidiary. The VegasWinners homepage says it is preparing to move from web sales to email VIP deals. Treat Root as a famous seller with marketing records, not a proven winner. If you buy, buy one pick at a time and keep your own record.

guarantee: VegasWinners.com does not sell a guarantee. The full refund policy, unchanged on 20 Nov 2026, reads: "No refunds, but credit applied in specific individual cases." It does not say which cases. The terms of service add that there are no guaranteed winners and that the site does not guarantee a winner from any picks sold. Picks appear in a member dashboard right after purchase, according to the delivery policy.

That is a change in tone from his earlier business. A Columbia Magazine profile from Fall 2008 said Root sold his picks as "Guaranteed Winners!" for as much as $25,000 for a season package. Older forum posts describe how make goods worked then: a TheRX member wrote in 2003 that after Root's free Super Bowl pick lost, a staffer from his office offered discounted picks rather than money back.

claims_note: How we checked: VegasWinners publishes no pick log, so the only record we can test the claims against is the seller's own pages, filings and releases. We compared dates, redid the percentages, and compared the profile on 7 Nov and 20 Nov 2026. The numbers mostly compute, but every one of them is a window or a category chosen by the seller, such as "Pinnacle" or "Gold Standard" plays, and the profile's season highlights stop in early 2020.

The numbers are also hard to square with Root's own words. In a 2004 Las Vegas Sun interview he said "the best gamblers in the world win 55 percent of their games overall" and that hitting 70 or 80 percent cannot be done. His pages lead with 68% to 75% runs. In a 2004 Daily Racing Form article, Root called himself "an entertainer and a salesman".

The streak lines we quoted from the homepage on 7 Nov, such as 28 and 12 and 2 over three weeks, were gone on 20 Nov. In their place was the day's pick, which opened with an admission of an 0 and 2 day. That is more candid than most sales copy, but it also shows how quickly a homepage record changes and why a buyer needs the full log.
record: Watchdog search, 22 Nov 2026: we searched about 1.37 million captured public posts from X, Reddit, Covers, TheRX and other forums for Wayne Allyn Root plays that were posted or reposted before a game started. We found 1 posts naming Wayne Allyn Root, but none carried a play we could match to a game and grade.

What is independently verifiable: very little about results. Root's past business is on public record. A 10-KSB annual report filed with the SEC for the year ended 31 Jul 2007 shows Winning Edge International, with Root as chairman and chief executive, sold sports handicapping advice through a subsidiary, reported revenue of $5,863,137 and a net loss of $1,198,504 that year, and sold all of its operating assets to Betbrokers PLC in September 2007. Those filings describe the business, not whether the picks won.

What is the seller's own marketing: every win and loss figure on VegasWinners.com, from the profile streaks to the 2017 to 2020 highlights. We found no full, searchable archive of his past picks with the line and post time, and no current season record.

The company today: the October 2026 SEC offering statement for Winners, Inc. says it acquired about 97% of VegasWinners, Inc. in August 2020, hired Root as chief executive on 1 Jul 2023 at $10,000 a month for three years, and on 30 Sep 2025 reorganized around MoneyLine Sports, a sports analytics company. It calls itself "a pre-revenue early development-stage company", reports unaudited gambling service revenue of $13,244 for 2023 and $6,797 for 2024, revenue of $594 and a net loss of $133,275 for the first half of 2026, and cash of $24,600 on 30 Jun 2026, and it says there is doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern. A December 2025 release named B. Michael Friedman chief executive, "with Wayne Allyn Root remaining as strategic advisor." Root is not listed among the officers in the October 2026 filing.

Root's public profile today is mostly political media. Wikipedia lists him as the 2008 Libertarian Party nominee for vice president and the host of national radio and TV talk shows. We found no court or regulator action involving his handicapping business in our searches.

our_data.text: In this edition Wayne Allyn Root is not matched to a Watchdog graded record, so we make no claim about how his picks perform.
our_data.context: For scale: Root's pages lead with 68% to 75% runs.

customers_intro: We found no review site entries from people who bought Root's picks. The buyer evidence is a 2015 Covers thread opened by a member who said they had just lost money on Root's service, a 2023 TheRX thread where subscribers argued about what he sent, and older forum posts from 2003 to 2009 about his TV show and sales methods.

customers.text: We read about 15 forum posts about Root from 2003 to 2023 on Sportsbook Review, TheRX and Covers. The pattern has been steady for two decades: members doubt his win rates, say his sales pitch outruns his results, and complain about follow up sales calls. The most direct buyer report is from Covers in November 2015, where a member said they were down $1,775 after a 4 and 12 run since Thanksgiving; another member in that thread said they quit the service after three weeks about ten years earlier and still got sales calls. A 2003 TheRX member said a losing free pick was followed by an offer of discounted picks. On the other side, two 2023 subscribers on TheRX discussed his plays without calling him a loss, and a 2009 member said the free TV picks from shows like his usually hit more than 50%. We found no buyer posting a tracked record of his picks, and no Reddit thread from a buyer.

Trustpilot had no page for vegaswinners.com, a Better Business Bureau search for VegasWinners returned no business, and we found no app store listing. In the Reddit betting forum posts we could search through the Arctic Shift archive on 20 Nov 2026, including searches for VegasWinners, we found no post from someone who bought Root's picks. Several archive searches timed out, so a Reddit comment could be missing.

On TheRX forum, two members who each said they had a year long subscription to Root argued over the previous day's picks. One said Root's site showed only one play; the other said Root also emails subscribers a bonus play and more plays, and that he does not keep his site well updated. If so, what the site shows may not match what subscribers receive.
In the same thread another member said they did not know who bets Root's picks and that buyers would do better spending that money on a different service. They gave no results.

On the Sportsbook Review forum, the member who opened a thread about the Winning Edge TV show called its handicappers salesmen and frauds, and a later post in the thread called Root a liar. No evidence about specific picks or customers was given.
In the same thread a member listed each handicapper's best bet of the week from the previous day's show and said all of them lost, including Root's Colorado State pick. That is one week of picks.

In a Sportsbook Review thread about TV handicapping shows, a member who strongly disliked Root posted what they said was a promotional email from Root, saying his business had gone "100% web" through WinningEDGE.com and VegasWINNERS.com. Another member claimed Winning Edge had gone bankrupt; SEC filings show the company sold its assets in 2007.
In the same thread a member said they tracked the free picks from these shows and they usually hit more than 50%, but that they had never called the hotline or bought picks.

On the Covers forum, a member opened a thread to say they were down $1,775 since joining Root's handicapping service, which they said had gone 4 and 12 since Thanksgiving, and warned others to think twice before paying. Later in the thread they called buying picks a foolish decision. We could not check their count.
In the same thread, another member said they bought Root's service about ten years earlier, quit after three weeks, and was still getting sales calls.
Other members in the thread argued that paid picks are no better than doing your own work, and one said Root's picks could be found online for free. These are opinions, not results.

On TheRX, a member said they lost money betting a free Raiders pick Root gave on CNN before a Super Bowl, and that a staffer from Root's office later offered discounted picks as a make good. They advised others to stay away.

In the same thread, replying to a promotional profile of Root, a member alleged that his public company spent more than it earned and that he bought his TV and radio airtime rather than earning it with results. SEC filings from the period do show losses; the airtime claim is unproven.

conflicts: VegasWinners is a sportsbook affiliate. A 2021 press release from the parent said it "intends to drive traffic to gaming operators for commission", and a 2022 Sportsbook Review article said BetMGM, Unibet and Rush Street Interactive had agreed to pay it for referrals. On 7 Nov 2026 the homepage loaded a BetMGM partner banner. A pick seller that earns from sportsbooks gains when readers bet more, win or lose.

VegasWinners also sells picks from other handicappers, and the parent is a publicly quoted stock. Its press releases, such as the 2021 "over 73%" release, promote both the picks and the company, and Root's own employment was tied to that company.
strengths: A named company, a customer service phone number and email, and a written delivery policy explaining where purchased picks appear.
Single picks cost $30, so a buyer can test one pick without a large package.
The terms state plainly that there are no guaranteed winners, which is more honest than his old "Guaranteed Winners!" pitch.
His past and present businesses are documented in public SEC filings, including the losses.
His daily write up admits bad days in plain words, as the 20 Nov 2026 pick did with its "0-2" opening.
concerns: No full public record. Every figure on the site is a streak or season highlight chosen by the seller, and the profile's highlights stop in 2020.
No refunds. Credit is offered only in unnamed "specific individual cases".
Subscription and VIP prices are not shown, and the subscription link did not load.

The parent company calls itself pre revenue, reported $594 of revenue in the first half of 2026 and doubts it can continue as a going concern, while the site still lists picks dated 2023 and 2024 and calls Root CEO.
The site is a sportsbook affiliate, paid when readers sign up at partner books.
The only direct buyer report we found, from 2015, described a losing run and sales calls that continued for years.
checklist: Ask for every pick from the last 12 months with the line, the odds and the time it was sent. A list of hot runs is not a record.
Get any VIP email price in writing before you pay, and ask what happens if the service stops during the season.
Count units, not wins. A 60% record at heavy favorites can still lose money.
Remember there are no refunds. Buy one $30 pick at a time rather than a long package.
Do not sign up at a sportsbook through the site because a pick seller suggested it.
faq: He is a real, well known handicapper with a documented business history, and VegasWinners.com sells his picks with a listed phone number and terms. We could not verify that his picks win over time, because the site publishes no full record.
How much does Wayne Allyn Root cost?
On 20 Nov 2026 his single picks on VegasWinners.com were $30 each. The homepage offers VIP email packages through April by request but shows no price, and the subscription link did not load.
Does Wayne Allyn Root have a verified record?

No. The win rates on his pages, such as 28 and 13 in the 2019 NBA playoffs or a 7 and 1 Pinnacle streak, are the seller's own figures with no log behind them, and a 2021 claim of independent monitoring named no monitor.
Is Wayne Allyn Root still CEO of VegasWinners?
Not of the parent. Winners, Inc. named B. Michael Friedman chief executive in late 2025 and said Root stays on as strategic advisor. The VegasWinners About Us page still calls Root CEO.

SEC filings show Winning Edge International, which Root chaired, sold its operating assets to Betbrokers PLC in September 2007. Root later sold picks through VegasWinners, which Winners, Inc. bought in 2020.
Is Wayne Allyn Root worth it?

For $30 you get one pick from a famous handicapper with a short write up. What is unproven is whether his picks beat the roughly 52.4% needed at -110 over hundreds of bets, and the site gives no refunds if they lose.
